original_question: What is the extremely rare autosomal dominant disorder, reported in only ten families worldwide, that is characterized by the absence of fingerprints, the development of blisters and facial milia shortly after birth, and is caused by mutations in the SMARCAD1 gene on chromosome 4?

final_qi.short_answer: absence of fingerprints-congenital milia syndrome (Baird syndrome)
final_qi.long_answer: The disorder is known as absence of fingerprints-congenital milia syndrome, also commonly referred to as Baird syndrome. It is an extremely rare autosomal dominant condition that has been reported in only ten families worldwide. Individuals with this syndrome present with an absence of fingerprints, the occurrence of blisters, and the development of facial milia shortly after birth. The condition stems from mutations in a skin-specific isoform of the SMARCAD1 gene located on chromosome 4, which plays a role in the development of fingerprint patterns. This mutation disrupts normal skin development, leading to the clinical features observed in the disorder.

Section: Introduction
Absence of fingerprints-congenital milia syndrome, also known simply as Baird syndrome is an extremely rare autosomal dominant genetic disorder which is characterized by a lack of fingerprints and the appearance of blisters and facial milia soon after birth.[2] It has been described in ten families worldwide.[3][4]
Section: Presentation
People with this disorder often have congenital adermatoglyphia, facial milia and blisters soon after birth, hypohidrosis (less sweating than average), and either thin or thickened skin throughout the body.[5][6][7][8] Single transversal palmar lines, plantar keratoderma, nail grooving, toe syndactyly and finger camptodactyly have also been reported.[9][10][11] Rarely, constriction ring syndrome is reported.[12] Single transversal palmar lines, plantar keratoderma, nail grooving, toe syndactyly and finger camptodactyly have also been reported.[9][10][11] Rarely, constriction ring syndrome is reported.[12]
Section: Causes
Through a large Han Chinese family with the disorder, it was found to be caused by mutations in the SMARCAD1 gene, in chromosome 4.[13][14][15][16][17][18][19] This gene produces a protein that is believed to control genes associated with the development of the fingerprints.[20]
